newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuba confirms its diplomats among freed hostages in Peru.
newsitem.headline: Cuba confirms its diplomats among freed hostages in Peru.

text.p: Cuba on Monday confirmed that two Cuban diplomats were among 225 people freed on Sunday by Marxist rebels holding hostages at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima.

A Foreign Ministry statement published by state news agencies said Cuba's ambassador to Peru, Pedro Diaz, and the embassy's number two, Jose Raul Silva, were among the hostages released late Sunday. It said they were in good physical and mental condition.

The statement noted the rebels were still holding more than 100 hostages and were still demanding concessions from the government of Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori. Officials at the Cuban Foreign Ministry were not available to comment any further on the statement.
The Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels were holding about 140 hostages at the residence on Monday.
Cuba refrained from condemning the attack on the residence. The Foreign Ministry has said only that it was following the situation closely and was in contact with Peruvian authorities.
Ministry officials declined any comment on speculation Cuba might be called on, or might offer, to mediate in the crisis.
The MRTA is said to be inspired by Cuba's revolution but it was not known to have any links with Havana.

President Fidel Castro mediated last June to secure the freedom from kidnapping by a Colombian guerrilla group of the brother of former Colombian president Cesar Gaviria. Some of the kidnappers and their families flew to Cuba.
Havana also intervened to help resolve a crisis in Colombia in 1980 when guerrillas of the M-19 movement seized 14 ambassadors at the Dominican embassy residence in Bogota.
That siege lasted two months and ended without bloodshed when the guerrillas dropped their demands and freed their hostages, flying to Cuba in a plane sent by Castro.
